lessons.title: A supplementary-file download can return an HTML page saved under the expected filename
lessons.description: A landing page, consent interstitial or bot-block answers with 200 and the client saves it as the requested name, so the parse failure surfaces several steps later.
lessons.cues: Fetching a supplementary or data file from a journal, a repository landing page, or a DOI link.

applies_to.tested: local download of journal supplementary files

evidence.method: the file was later found to be HTML or XML

sections.symptom:
An `.xlsx` or `.tsv.gz` will not parse, or parses into nonsense, several steps after it was
fetched.
sections.cause:
Likely: the URL was a landing page, a login or consent interstitial, or a bot-block response, and
the client saved the body under the requested name with a 200.
sections.check_first:
Right after any download: file size, leading bytes (zip or gzip magic versus `<`), and
content-type if available.
sections.intervention:
Find the direct file URL, or have Galaxy fetch it server-side; if access is gated, tell the user
rather than working around it.
sections.validate: The file opens as its claimed type and has the expected shape: sheets, columns, row count.
sections.not_when: The file is genuinely the right type and the parse error is about its contents.

lessons.title: "History is not accessible by user" means there is no data to reason from
lessons.description: A 403 on the bound history means nothing about the job was ever read, so any explanation of the failure after that point is invented.

signatures: History is not accessible by user

lessons.cues: A resumed notebook is bound to a history that the current credentials do not own.

applies_to.tested: resumed notebook bound to a history owned by another account

evidence.method: transcript: a 403 followed by a fabricated explanation of a job failure

graduated_to: loom system prompt no-fabrication rule plus evals

sections.symptom: Asked why a job failed, the agent gets a 403 on the history and answers anyway.
sections.cause:
The notebook's bound history belongs to a different account or server than the current
credentials. Nothing about the job was ever read.
sections.check_first: Which account are the current credentials for? Is the bound history in that account's list?
sections.intervention: Report the access failure. Offer to look in the user's own recent histories instead.
sections.validate: Any explanation of a failure cites a job or dataset that was actually retrieved.
sections.not_when: Never; a 403 is always a hard stop for reasoning about that history.

lessons.title: A collection handed to a single-dataset input is rejected; the answer is map-over, not "the API cannot"
lessons.description: A 400 at submit when an hdca meets a single-dataset parameter means map-over was not requested, and the wrong conclusion is that collections cannot be used through the API.

signatures: supplied to single input dataset parameter

lessons.cues: A collection is being passed where the tool's input template says one dataset.

evidence.method: the batch wrapper form was accepted by Galaxy and produced a mapped-over output collection

graduated_to: loom context.ts Galaxy block map-over hint

sections.symptom:
400 at submit when an `hdca` is passed where the tool expects one dataset. Observed follow-on: the
agent concludes collections cannot be built or used through the API, which is false.
sections.cause:
The input is a single-dataset parameter. Galaxy runs such a tool over a collection only when asked
to map over it.
sections.check_first:
Is the input really single-dataset per the tool's input template, and is the thing being passed a
collection? If the collection is `list:paired` and the tool wants one sample, map-over is still the
answer but the element type must match.
sections.intervention: Submit the input in batch form: `{batch: true, values: [{src: "hdca", id: <collection id>}]}`.
sections.validate:
The result is a collection with one element per input element, and element identifiers are
preserved.
sections.not_when: The tool has a genuine multi-dataset or collection input -- pass the collection directly there.

lessons.title: "ConnectedValue object at 0x" in a command line means an optional workflow parameter was left unset
lessons.description: Older Galaxy serialized the placeholder object's repr into the command line when a connected optional parameter_input had no value, so the step can fail or silently succeed wrong.
lessons.cues: A workflow with optional parameter inputs is invoked against a server older than the upstream fix.

evidence.method: the error string was quoted from the failing job and the upstream fix was identified

sections.symptom:
A workflow step fails, or worse succeeds, with a tool argument containing the text
`...ConnectedValue object at 0x...`. With fastp it surfaced as an invalid adapter sequence.
sections.cause:
An optional `parameter_input` workflow step was connected but given no value; older Galaxy
serialized the placeholder object's repr into the command line.
sections.check_first:
Does the workflow have optional parameter inputs, per the workflow details? Is the server older
than the fix? Inspect the failed job's command line for the signature.
sections.intervention: Pass an explicit empty value for every optional parameter input on invocation.
sections.validate:
Re-inspect the command line of the rerun job: the signature is gone AND the argument is absent or
empty, not replaced by some other junk.
sections.not_when:
The server has the upstream fix. Keep the lesson and narrow the version range -- older installs
still need it.

lessons.title: The number shown in the history panel is not a dataset id
lessons.description: Users say "dataset 28", which is the hid; the API wants the encoded id, and run_tool reports the mismatch as a misleading missing-parameter error.

signatures: Invalid id length, must be multiple of 16

lessons.cues: A short numeric identifier taken from what the user said is being passed where the API wants an encoded id.

evidence.method: reproduced; resolving the hid to the encoded id fixed it

sections.symptom:
An id-length error, or -- from run_tool -- a misleading required-parameter error that says nothing
about ids.
sections.cause: Users say "dataset 28"; that is the `hid`. The API wants the encoded `id`.
sections.check_first: Is the id being passed short and numeric?
sections.intervention:
List the history contents and resolve the hid to an id. Confirm the name matches what the user
meant.
sections.validate: The call succeeds and the returned dataset's name and hid are the intended ones.
sections.not_when: The id is already a 16-hex-multiple string -- then the missing-parameter error has another cause.

lessons.title: Workflow input values, scalars included, go in `inputs`; `params` only overrides tool steps
lessons.description: A validation error pointing into parameters means the value is in the wrong slot, not under the wrong key, and retrying key forms is the trap that follows.

signatures: Input should be a valid dictionary

lessons.cues: A workflow invocation is being retried with different key forms for the same value.

applies_to.tested: galaxy-mcp invoke_workflow against a multi-sample IWC workflow

evidence.method: the same values succeeded first try when moved to inputs per the input template

sections.symptom:
Invocation rejected with a validation error pointing into `parameters`. Observed: a model retried
two dozen times varying the key -- label, step index, uuid -- while the real problem was the slot.
sections.cause:
Inferred, not checked against Galaxy source: every workflow input -- datasets, collections and
scalar parameter inputs alike -- belongs in `inputs`. `params` overrides tool parameters on
non-input steps and its values are dicts.
sections.check_first: Was the workflow input template fetched? Does the failing payload put a scalar under `params`?
sections.intervention:
Fetch the input template and fill it in as returned. Do not retry with a different key form; if the
second attempt fails the same way, stop and re-read the template.
sections.validate: The invocation is accepted and its recorded inputs match what was intended.
sections.not_when: You really are overriding a tool step's parameter -- then `params` with a dict value is right.

lessons.title: Repeat-group tool params written with underscores are accepted but silently mis-applied
lessons.description: Galaxy's flat parameter form addresses repeat members with a pipe; an underscore key is ignored rather than rejected, so the repeat falls back to defaults and the job still reports ok.
lessons.cues: Tool inputs contain keys shaped like name underscore number underscore field.

evidence.method: a wrong aggregate was observed; the pipe-form keys produced the expected one

sections.symptom:
A tool with a repeat block runs to `ok`, but the result reflects default or wrong repeat values --
a different operation or column than requested. No error anywhere.
sections.cause:
Hypothesized: Galaxy's flat parameter form addresses repeat members as `block_0|field`. A key like
`block_0_field` is not rejected; it is ignored, and the repeat falls back to defaults.
sections.check_first:
Look at the inputs actually submitted. Any repeat member addressed with an underscore instead of a
pipe? Compare the job's recorded parameters with what was intended.
sections.intervention:
Use the pipe form, for example `operations_0|op_name`, preferably taken verbatim from the tool's
input template rather than constructed by hand.
sections.validate:
Read back the job's parameters and confirm the repeat values are the requested ones. Spot-check one
output value by hand.
sections.not_when:
The tool errored at submit -- that is a different problem. Conditionals use the same pipe
addressing but fail differently.

lessons.title: A successful run_tool response means queued, not finished
lessons.description: Single-tool submission returns at queue time and there is no invocation object to poll, so nothing prompts the second look before the result is reported.
lessons.cues: About to report a tool run as done.

evidence.method: the job was later found in an error state after the agent had reported success

sections.symptom: The agent reports an analysis step complete; the job is still running or has since errored.
sections.cause:
Single-tool submission returns at queue time. Unlike a workflow invocation there is no invocation
object to poll, so nothing prompts a second look.
sections.check_first:
Has the job reached a terminal state? `ok` is success; `error`, `failed` and `deleted` are not;
`paused` and `waiting` are not terminal.
sections.intervention: Poll the job to a terminal state before building on its outputs or reporting it.
sections.validate: Terminal `ok`, and the expected outputs exist and are non-empty.
sections.not_when:
Never. Caveat: reaching the job via an output dataset does not work for jobs with no outputs,
collection-only outputs, or map-over runs where one call makes many jobs.

lessons.title: A tool's built-in reference option is useless on a server that has no indexes for it
lessons.description: The cached-reference branch of a tool offers nothing when the server's data table is empty, and through a workflow the invocation validates and every sample fails minutes later.

signatures: requires a value, but no legal values defined

lessons.cues: The tool offers a choice between a cached or built-in reference and one from the history.

applies_to.versions: any; depends on the server's data tables
applies_to.tested: STARsolo on a server with no STAR indexes

evidence.method: the 400 at submit was quoted, and the server was confirmed to have zero indexes for the tool

sections.symptom:
`Parameter 'genomeDir': requires a value, but no legal values defined` at submit. Through a
workflow it is worse: the invocation validates, and the failure shows up minutes later as a bare
tool error on every sample.
sections.cause:
The use-a-built-in-index branch of the tool was selected, and this server's data table for that
tool is empty.
sections.check_first: Does the select parameter for the built-in reference have any options on this server?
sections.intervention:
Switch to the history-reference branch and supply a FASTA, and an annotation where the tool needs
one, or run on a server that has the index.
sections.validate:
The job reaches `ok`, and the mapping rate is plausible for the organism -- a wrong reference also
"works".
sections.not_when: The select has options and the chosen value is not among them -- that is a wrong-value problem.

lessons.title: A faithful rerun can still be wrong when a normalizing step was fed a pre-filtered subset
lessons.description: A statistic normalized over its input is wrong if the input was hand-picked, and the rerun reproduces the error exactly, so provenance alone will never catch it.
lessons.cues: Reproducing a published analysis where a step computes a normalized quantity -- posterior, FDR, enrichment, rank, percentile.

applies_to.tested: one audited reproduction of a fine-mapping analysis

evidence.method: traced by reading the job's actual inputs; the denominator differed from the full set

sections.symptom:
Results are close to the paper's but not equal: a set has a few members more or fewer, and every
downstream value drifts by a few percent in the same direction.
sections.cause:
A statistic normalized over its input, here posterior probabilities, was computed over a
hand-picked subset. The tool ran correctly. Rerunning reproduces the error, so provenance alone
will not catch it.
sections.check_first:
For every normalizing step: how many records went in, and how many does the method assume? Compare
against the paper's stated N.
sections.intervention: Feed the step the full population; filter afterwards.
sections.validate: Input count matches the method's stated population, and the set membership matches the paper.
sections.not_when: The step's output for one record does not depend on the others.

lessons.title: When a rerun cannot find what the paper reports, compare the Methods parameters to the executed ones
lessons.description: A missing peak or row, or a uniform few-percent drift with ranks intact, is usually a window, threshold, top-N or version difference rather than a failed reproduction.
lessons.cues: Reproducing a published analysis where a reported feature, row or peak is absent from the rerun.

evidence.method: each discrepancy traced to a specific parameter or version difference

sections.symptom:
A table row, peak or feature from the paper is not in the rerun's output at all; or scores are
systematically a few percent off with ranks preserved.
sections.cause:
Four observed varieties: a window or range parameter narrower than the Methods describe, so the
feature lies outside what was scanned; a summary step's top-N or threshold dropping it; a tool
revision changing output columns; a model or tool version change shifting values uniformly.
sections.check_first:
Tabulate Methods-stated versus executed values for windows, thresholds, top-N limits and versions.
Is the missing item outside a range or below a cutoff? Is the drift uniform with ranks intact?
sections.intervention:
Rerun with the Methods' parameters if they differ. If versions differ and cannot be matched, report
the drift as version drift, with its size, rather than as a failed reproduction.
sections.validate:
The missing item appears under the Methods' parameters, or its absence is explained by a named
parameter. Say which.
sections.not_when:
Parameters and versions match and the result still differs -- that is a real discrepancy; report
it.

lessons.title: Fold-change signs read backwards and sample labels drift, with no error anywhere
lessons.description: Factor-level order decides numerator and denominator, and upstream steps rewrite sample labels, so a DE result can be fully reversed or mis-assigned and still look clean.
lessons.cues: Building a design or factor table, and reporting log fold changes.

evidence.method: user reports across one analysis: duplicate labels, unstated sign convention, design that did not match the data

sections.symptom:
Fold-change signs read backwards; duplicate or dropped sample labels; a multi-sample design
applied to data that was actually pooled.
sections.cause:
Factor-level order decides numerator versus denominator and is easy to get implicitly. Sample
labels get rewritten by upstream steps. Nobody compared the design table to the data before
running.
sections.check_first:
Before running: one row per sample, labels unique, every sample in the design is in the data and
vice versa, replicates per condition as the design claims.
sections.intervention:
State the contrast in words -- treated relative to control, positive means up in treated -- in the
plan and again next to the results.
sections.validate: Pick a gene with a known direction and check its sign.
sections.not_when: Never; it holds for any two-group comparison.

lessons.title: Numeric filters in awk and friends treat "NA" as 0, so missing p-values pass a significance cutoff
lessons.description: DESeq2 writes NA for filtered genes; string-to-number coercion turns NA into 0, which is below any cutoff, so the significant count is inflated with no error.
lessons.cues: Thresholding a p-value or padj column with awk, cut/sort, or a Galaxy filter expression.

evidence.method: deterministic: NA plus 0 is 0 in awk; the count dropped to the expected range once NA rows were excluded

sections.symptom: Implausibly many significant genes -- several-fold more than expected. Nothing errors.
sections.cause:
DESeq2 writes `NA` for genes removed by independent filtering or outlier detection.
String-to-number coercion turns `NA` into 0, which is below any cutoff.
sections.check_first:
Count rows where the tested column is literally `NA`. If that count is close to the excess, this
is it.
sections.intervention:
Exclude NA explicitly before comparing, or do the filter in a language with real missing-value
semantics.
sections.validate: Significant count equals rows passing the cutoff among non-NA rows. State both numbers.
sections.not_when: The table has no missing values in that column.
